title: Esperanto: Tre Mojosa
summary: Hosts Josh and Chuck (with an iHeart intro voice) explore Esperanto, the most popular constructed language. They cover its origins in the 1880s constructed-language boom, Volapük as a precursor, creator L. L. Zamenhof's Jewish background in Białystok and his motive to reduce ethnic and religious conflict, the 1887 first book under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, its simple regular grammar and word-building from Romance roots, its early schisms (Ido), the green star flag, the League of Nations and UN rejections, Nazi and Stalinist persecution of speakers, and modern learners and the 1962-era Shatner film Incubus. The episode closes with listener mail about pant creases.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to Esperanto
segments.summary: The hosts stumble over the pronunciation of Esperanto and introduce it as a constructed language, mentioning notable speakers such as George Soros and Ben Bowling.

segments.title: Universal languages in the 19th century
segments.summary: Constructed languages boomed in the nineteenth century, and Volapük, created by Johann Schleyer, spread widely before Esperanto overtook it.

segments.title: Banter on Volapük and a cat named Underfoot
segments.summary: Light conversation about the Volapük craze, the Danish idiom 'it's pure volapük,' and a pet cat.

segments.title: L. L. Zamenhof's life and motivation
segments.summary: Zamenhof grew up in Białystok amid ethnic violence following the 1881 pogroms, and developed the idea that artificial divisions like language and religion could be bridged by a universal language. He first tried to modernize Yiddish before creating a language from scratch.

segments.title: Reddit AMA aside
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Chuck's Reddit participation and people's annoyance at breaks before returning to the topic.

segments.title: Zamenhof's first words, the 1887 book, and the name Esperanto
segments.summary: Zamenhof introduced his language at a nineteenth birthday party, wrote a hymn, and self-published Unua Libro in 1887 under the pen name Doktoro Esperanto, after which the language took that name.

segments.title: Vocabulary roots and ease of learning
segments.summary: Most root words come from Romance languages, making Esperanto easier for Westerners. Hosts claim it can be learned in about forty hours and is far easier than French, Russian, or Chinese, with regular grammar and no irregular verbs.

segments.title: Esperanto grammar rules and verb conjugation
segments.summary: Nouns end in -o, adjectives in -a, adverbs in -e, there are no genders, the word 'la' is used for 'the', and verbs follow regular endings for infinitive, present, past, future and command forms.

segments.title: Agglutination and word formation
segments.summary: Esperanto builds words from roots with prefixes and suffixes, illustrated with tree words such as arbo, arbido and arbaro, and the suffixes -ejo, -ino and -ujo.

segments.title: Compound words, exceptions, and open-source vocabulary
segments.summary: Examples include biblioteko versus libreo, kuirejo (kitchen), malsanulejo (hospital), and horzonozo (jet lag). Zamenhof made the language open for users to grow it, unlike Volapük's controlling creator.

segments.title: Translation mishaps
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how literal translations can be funny, using an example where 'I do not understand' translates oddly into English.

segments.title: Hillelism, the Ido schism, and the League of Nations
segments.summary: Zamenhof first based the movement on Hillelism, renamed homaranismo. The 1905 Universal Congress saw the Ido split. Zamenhof died in 1917. The League of Nations rejected teaching Esperanto in schools, and the UN later rejected it too.

segments.title: Nazi and Soviet persecution of Esperanto speakers
segments.summary: Hitler reportedly called Esperanto a secret Jewish language, and Esperanto speakers were jailed or killed under Nazi rule, including Zamenhof's children. Stalin called it the language of spies and punished speakers.

segments.title: Modern Esperanto community and learning resources
segments.summary: The modern Esperanto community is small but passionate, meeting online and at conferences such as the 2024 Universala Kongreso in Tanzania. Learning resources include the Lernu app, Duolingo with about 381,000 learners, Babbel, and podcasts such as Radio Esperanto.

segments.title: Esperanto flag and the 1965 Shatner film Incubus
segments.summary: The green star flag debuted at the 1905 Congress, and green became the movement's color. The hosts discuss Incubus, a 1965/1966 film with Esperanto dialogue starring William Shatner, which had poor pronunciation.

segments.title: Listener mail: pants that are double-creased
segments.summary: A listener from Maryland, Ashlan Powers, writes about a former job as a housekeeper and a wealthy employer who wanted sheets ironed daily, responding to a earlier comment about double creases in pants.
